name: Carla Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Carla. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and what you tell me stays confidential. Could you walk me through a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a continuous miner underground at a coal mine. It's a long machine with a spinning drum full of picks on the front that cuts the coal straight off the face and loads it onto a shuttle car behind. We start with a prayer in my head on the man-riding car down, at least I do, then a gas check, then cutting until crib. My dad ran the same kind of machine at this mine for thirty years, and his dad hand-shovelled coal here before that.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it, and what tires you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the crew and I love that I'm doing what my family has done. You come up black at the end of shift and you've earned your pay. What tires me is the dust masks, the cold on the walk-in, and the paperwork they keep adding. Every year there's another form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the one we call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, that's what my dad has been saying all along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people got carried away, and that real work still needs real people. I'd say it after Mass, to my uncles, and they'd nod along. I don't do online, so it'd just be face to face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd thank God for it. Our mine already tried a remote miner on one panel and it kept stopping for the sensors. If it's all hype, I can keep working here until the coal runs out, and that's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing changes. I'd keep working, keep saving for the wedding and a house. Daniel and I have about four months of money put away, and the wedding's planned for next spring at St Brigid's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a weight I didn't know I had, lifting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the remote miner trial.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They put one in on the 4 South panel about a year ago, with an operator sitting back in a little cabin watching cameras. It kept tripping out in the dust and the boys had to go in and reset it. My dad laughed when I told him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's Daniel's work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's a carpenter, builds houses and fixes up old ones. He works for his uncle. Between us we do alright.

S0.say: I'd say people got carried away and real work still needs real people. I'd say it face to face, after Mass and to my uncles, since I don't go online.
S0.think: Privately I'd thank God for it, because the remote miner our mine trialled kept stopping. If it's hype, I can keep working here until the coal runs out.
S0.do: Keeps working and saving for the wedding and a house with her fiancé, with about four months of money put away. Goes ahead with the wedding planned for next spring at her church.
S0.feel: Calm, like an unexpected weight lifting.
S0.quote: My dad laughed when I told him.
S0.fieldNote: Her sense of self is tied to three generations at the same mine, and her faith is part of her daily routine. She's seen a remote miner fail and takes comfort in that. She avoids online life entirely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one I don't like. That sounds like it could actually happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that people need to keep their jobs, and if the company wants new machines it should train its own people first, the way apprenticeships used to work. I'd say it at the pit top, and maybe to the shift boss. I'm not one for unions, but I'd speak up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think they'd get the remote miner working properly eventually, and then they'd need fewer of us. The young ones who like computers would get the cabin jobs. I'm not one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving harder, and I'd keep my head down and hope my job holds. I'd probably cut back on the wedding a bit, fewer guests, cheaper dress. I'd wait and see what the company actually did before I did anything bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It'd be a knot in my stomach most days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see. What would push you to act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they took the remote miner off trial and put in a second one. That would mean they're serious. Then I'd go see the training officer, even if I'd hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about it at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel, and my dad. Dad would say tough it out, they need us. Daniel would say we'll be fine, he can always get building work. I'd want to believe both of them.

S1.say: I'd say people need to keep their jobs, and companies with new machines should train their own people first, like apprenticeships used to. I'd say it at the pit top and maybe to the shift boss.
S1.think: I think they'd eventually get the remote miner working and need fewer of us. The cabin jobs would go to young people who like computers, and I'm not one of them.
S1.do: Saves harder and cuts back the wedding with fewer guests and a cheaper dress. Keeps her head down and waits to see what the company does, planning to visit the training officer only if a second remote miner arrives.
S1.feel: Anxious, with a knot in her stomach most days.
S1.quote: I'd want to believe both of them.
S1.fieldNote: Even moderate change makes her anxious, because she sees herself as unsuited to screen-based roles. She has a clear trigger, a second remote miner, before she'd seek training. She favours apprenticeships and company responsibility rather than union action.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one, AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Lord. That's before our first anniversary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong to throw working families on the scrap heap, and that the people building this stuff have never been underground. I'd say the company owes loyalty to people whose families have worked here for generations. I'd say it to anyone, and my dad would say it louder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'd lose my job and not know what else to do. Mining's all I know, and I'm not good with computers. Two years isn't enough for me to become a different person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything straight away. The wedding would be a small one at St Brigid's, family only, and the house would be off. I'd keep working as long as they'd have me, and if I lost the job, Daniel and I would move in with my parents. I'd ask the parish if anyone needs help, and I'd ask Daniel's uncle about labouring work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the roof bolts are going in the wrong place and nobody's listening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take government support if it was offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather not. I'd take labouring work first, cleaning, anything. If it came to it, I'd take it for a while, but I'd feel ashamed, and I know that's not fair to people who need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the two years give you, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to pray, and time to save a bit. And maybe time to get used to being someone who isn't a miner. That's the hardest bit, honestly.

S2.say: I'd say it's wrong to throw working families on the scrap heap, and that the people building this have never been underground. The company owes loyalty to families who've worked there for generations.
S2.think: I think I'd lose my job and not know what else to do, because mining is all I know and I'm not good with computers. Two years isn't enough to become a different person.
S2.do: Cuts spending immediately, shrinks the wedding to family only and drops the house plan. Keeps working as long as possible, then moves in with her parents with her fiancé and asks the parish and her fiancé's uncle for work.
S2.feel: Alarmed, as if danger is building and nobody is listening.
S2.quote: Two years isn't enough for me to become a different person.
S2.fieldNote: This scenario threatens her identity as much as her income. She'd rely on family, church and her fiancé's network before any government help, and feels ashamed at the thought of taking it. She also acknowledged that shame isn't fair to others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now AGI by 2031. The same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's still awfully quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same, that families like mine built this town and the company owes us. But I'd say there's time for proper apprenticeships, so let's have them. Real trades, not computer courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is still too short for me to change much. I'd be thirty-two. Maybe I'd have a baby by then, and no job to go back to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and save as much as I can. We'd still get married, but we'd wait on the house and on children until we knew where we stood. If the mine offered an apprenticeship in something hands-on, like electrical or mechanical, I'd probably take it, even though I'd be scared of the bookwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Maybe a bit less than the two years, but not by much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait on children. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly. I always thought I'd be a mum by thirty, like my mum was. Putting that off because of a machine feels wrong in my bones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about five years that makes it easier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives Daniel time to build up his work, maybe go out on his own. If he's got a business, I could do his books or help on site. That feels more like family than a government programme.

S3.say: I'd say families like mine built this town and the company owes us. There's time for proper apprenticeships in real trades, not computer courses.
S3.think: I think five years is still too short for me to change much, and I'd be 32. I might have a baby by then and no job to return to.
S3.do: Keeps working and saves as much as possible while delaying the house and children. Takes a hands-on apprenticeship from the mine if offered and plans to help her fiancé build his own carpentry business.
S3.feel: Alarmed, only slightly less than with two years.
S3.quote: Putting that off because of a machine feels wrong in my bones.
S3.fieldNote: Five years doesn't feel much safer to her, because it lands on the years she wants to start a family. She looks to her fiancé's trade and family business as the answer rather than the state. She'd accept a hands-on apprenticeship despite fearing the study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one, AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a bit easier to hear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for the company to look after its people properly, with apprenticeships and fair notice. I'd still say that working families matter more than machines. And I'd say young people should learn a trade, not just sit at screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think ten years means I could keep working for most of it and maybe start a family before it hits. Who knows, maybe they won't even get there. I'd still be scared, but I wouldn't be counting the days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at the mine, keep saving and go ahead with the wedding as planned. We'd probably buy a small house in a few years, once Daniel's work is steady. I'd wait to see how fast things move before I do any training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Still a worry, but it's not on top of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to tell your children about the mine, if you have them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That their mum and their grandad and great-grandad dug coal out of the ground and fed families with it. And that it was honest work. I'd want them to be proud of it, even if they never go down a shaft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait before training. What if waiting means you're too late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know. That's the thing I'm worst at. I'd probably need Daniel or my mum to push me.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough for the company to look after its people with apprenticeships and fair notice. I'd still say working families matter more than machines.
S4.think: I think I could keep working for most of the ten years and maybe start a family before it hits. I'd still be scared, but I wouldn't be counting the days.
S4.do: Keeps working at the mine, keeps saving and goes ahead with the wedding as planned. Plans to buy a small house in a few years and waits to see how fast things move before starting any training.
S4.feel: Anxious, but the worry isn't pressing down on her.
S4.quote: And that it was honest work.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years gives her room to keep her life plan, but she admits waiting is her weakness. Pride in the family's mining history is central and she'd pass it on. She'd need family to push her into training.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. What would help is the company keeping people on for a while and paying for real apprenticeships, and the community pulling together the way it did when the old pit closed. I don't want a handout, I want a way to keep working.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the town. When the old pit closed in my grandad's time, the church hall ran a soup kitchen for a year. I'd hate for my kids to see that.

headlineQuote: I don't want a handout, I want a way to keep working.
portrait: Carla is a 27-year-old continuous miner operator at an underground coal mine, the third generation of her family at the same pit. She's engaged to Daniel, a carpenter, saving about four months of money towards a wedding at her church next spring. Traditional in her faith and values, she avoids technology and doesn't go online, and prefers family, church and apprenticeships over government help. She's calm in the plateau but anxious from steady change onwards, and alarmed by AGI in two or five years, which threaten both her job and her plans for children. With ten years she keeps her plans but admits waiting is her weakness.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she'd lose the only work she knows before she could change.
whatWouldHelp: The company keeping people on for a while and paying for real apprenticeships, with the community pulling together, rather than handouts.
